title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a preregistered, confirmatory experiment comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) against an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline) for intent-driven network-configuration tasks. The study used a paired design over N=120 intent→configuration tasks executed against a deterministic emulator-based validator; a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini) produced all candidate configurations. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired reduction in emulator-observed semantic failures. All 120 paired observations produced valid configurations in both conditions (baseline success rate = 1.00; guarded success rate = 1.00). The paired difference estimate = 0.00 (exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]). Confirmatory evidence therefore does not support a benefit for the guarded pipeline on this task set under the tested configuration. We report the full preregistration identifier and artifact locations, distinguish confirmatory and exploratory inferences, and discuss limitations—especially task generation, single-model scope, and external validity—and implications for future, production-focused evaluation of agentic NetOps systems.

sections.introduction: Automating network-operations tasks with large language models (LLMs) promises operational productivity gains but raises well-documented reliability and safety concerns: LLM-produced configuration changes can be syntactically plausible yet semantically harmful for live networks. Prior work recommends integrating verification or digital-twin validation into generation workflows (generate→validate→repair) or constraining LLMs to translation roles paired with verified solvers to reduce risk. Motivated by these recommendations, we preregistered and executed a confirmatory experiment asking: Does inserting an executable emulator-based validator into a generate→validate→repair loop reduce semantic/network-level failures of LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment (N=120 tasks) comparing the two workflows under a fixed model and harness; (2) a deterministic execution artifact set (hosted LLM calls, emulator traces, validators) archived under the preregistration; (3) a transparent report of confirmatory results (no observed difference) and a bounded discussion of operational implications and limitations.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and benchmarks document both promise and failure modes of LLMs in NetOps. Benchmarks that execute generated configurations in emulation or formal verification (e.g., Cornetto, NetConfArena) reveal semantic regressions and protocol-dependent failures not visible from syntax-only evaluation. Tool-augmented architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, runtime validation) are repeatedly proposed to improve safety, while position arguments advocate confining LLMs to translation-to-formal-model roles and delegating reasoning to verified solvers to enable auditable correctness. Our study was designed against this background to provide a preregistered, executable test of whether an emulator-based guarded loop yields fewer semantic failures than an LLM-only baseline on a curated task set.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental design: We preregistered study CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 before observing outcomes. The confirmatory question and analysis plan used a paired binary design with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks. Each task produced two episodes: baseline (LLM-only suggestion applied to the emulator) and guarded (LLM suggestion passed through a generate→validate→repair pipeline that could propose a single repair iteration). The LLM and prompting: all candidate configurations were produced by gpt-5-mini (hosted); prompts, seeds, and adapter settings were frozen per the preregistration. Execution harness: a deterministic emulator-based validator executed and checked candidate configurations against task-specific intent constraints and safety/workflow policies (e.g., make-before-break, shutdown→change→restore). The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in semantic-failure rate (guarded minus baseline), tested with an exact two-sided McNemar test; secondary outcomes included model-call counts and failure-mode taxonomy. Stopping, contamination, missingness, and sensitivity rules were preregistered; technical failures were to be logged and excluded from the primary analysis.
sections.results: Execution and primary outcome: The run completed under the preregistered harness (execution manifest available). All planned episodes completed: 240 episodes (120 pairs); model_calls_used = 120 (one shared initial generation per task). Validator scoring (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) reported valid configurations for every episode. In the paired contingency: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (guarded=1 & baseline=1 for all pairs). Baseline success rate = 1.00; guarded success rate = 1.00; paired difference estimate = 0.00. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0 (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00], bootstrap resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Secondary and exploratory analyses: preregistered secondary summaries (mean model calls per successful task; repair-iteration counts) are empty because no repairs were applied (repair_applied=false for all guarded episodes) and no additional model calls were consumed beyond the single shared generation per task per the execution log. Missingness and contamination: no episodes were excluded and contamination detectors did not flag any episodes under the preregistered checks.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The confirmatory result is a null difference: on this curated task set and harness, the guarded generate→validate→repair loop produced no observable reduction in emulator-observed semantic failures relative to the LLM-only workflow because the baseline already produced valid configurations for every task. This outcome is evidence about the joint system as executed (model, prompts, task generator, validator) and should not be read as a general statement that guarded loops are unnecessary in broader operational settings. Plausible explanations for the null effect include: (1) the task generator produced deterministic, well-scoped synthetic tasks whose intents mapped closely to the LLM’s prompt-conditioned capability; (2) the chosen prompt and single-generation budget sufficed for these tasks; (3) the single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and frozen prompting reduced variance compared with more adversarial or out-of-distribution scenarios. Operational implication: a guarded loop can still provide independent benefits in more heterogeneous, noisy, or adversarial production environments (as prior work shows), but our confirmatory evidence demonstrates that, for the tested synthetic task bank and model/prompt configuration, the additional validator/repair machinery did not change semantic-outcome rates.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, paired confirmatory experiment comparing an emulator-validated generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only suggestion workflow across 120 curated intent→configuration tasks. Results showed no difference: both conditions produced valid configurations in all episodes under the deterministic validator (paired difference estimate = 0.00; exact McNemar p = 1.0). This finding is narrowly scoped to the tested task set, model (gpt-5-mini), prompt configuration, and deterministic emulator validator. We emphasize carefully that: (i) null results here do not overturn prior evidence demonstrating LLM failure modes in broader benchmarks, and (ii) future work should evaluate diverse production-rooted incident corpora, multiple models and prompting regimes, and higher-budget guarded workflows (including multi-iteration repairs and richer validators). We release the preregistration, execution artifacts, and analysis outputs to support replication and targeted follow-up evaluations that address external validity gaps identified below. The manuscript and artifacts reserve the full set of checksums and execution logs for reviewers and archivists (see Disclosure).

LLM(s) used: gpt-5-mini (hosted). Adapter/orchestration framework: adapter_family="hosted_netops_gvr_v1" (deterministic emulator-based validator and deterministic task generator). Deviations: none were recorded against the preregistered stopping, contamination, or missingness plans. The archived bundle provides checksums, logs, and a manifest to verify the described run.
limitations: Confirmatory scope: the result is confirmatory and narrowly scoped to the preregistered task set, single LLM (gpt-5-mini), prompt configuration, and deterministic emulator validator used in this run.

Task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic (publicly derivable) and may underrepresent the diversity, noise, and adversarial conditions of production incidents; external validity to live operational networks is therefore limited.
Model and prompt diversity: only one hosted model and a single frozen prompting strategy were tested; multi-model, prompt-ensemble, or higher-budget iterative repair regimes were not evaluated.

Validator fidelity: the emulator/validator is deterministic and intended to be reproducible; its representativeness of heterogeneous vendor behaviors and partial observability in production is limited.

Statistical ceiling: the baseline achieved perfect success on this task bank, producing a null result for the guarded intervention; this ceiling effect constrains inference about guarded-loop benefits in broader settings.
